sections.title: Practice: Finding a Participant

orientation.html:
Welcome to HMIS Clarity.

This is a practice copy. A few things look different, but every step you take here is the step you will take in the real system. Let me show you around.
What follows is a practice version of Clarity. It behaves the way the real system behaves. Everyone in it is invented. Nothing you do here touches a real record.
You will be given eight situations. Each one is a person standing in front of you and something they have told you. Your job is to find their record and, later, to prove it is the right one.

The practice roster holds three hundred people. The live system holds hundreds of thousands. A search that returns a readable handful here can return pages there. So the habit to build is to narrow the search before you scan, not to scroll page after page.
Add a second word and it narrows. Every word has to match, but each one may match a different field. A last name and the first few letters of a first name is usually enough.

It is not only names. A year of birth works. So does a full date. So do the last four digits of a Social Security Number. Often the only part somebody can remember, and enough on its own to cut a long list down.

And any of them combine. Name and year. Last name and the last four. A first name and a date. Every word you add has to match, so each one narrows what is left. That is how you get a page of results down to a handful you can actually read.
Opening a row opens their record. This is not anybody you will be asked for. It is just to show you the shape of the page before you need it.

The top half is who they are: name, date of birth, age, Social Security Number, and the quality codes beside each one. Those codes say how good the information is, and they are what tells you a record is thin rather than wrong.

Down the left are the rest of their record. Most are dimmed. Clicking a dimmed control does nothing at all, and each lesson clears the part it teaches. Location is open because where somebody has been contacted is often what settles who they are.
Every place they have been recorded, with the date and who wrote it down. If somebody tells you they have been sleeping under a bridge, this is where you find out whether the record agrees with them.
Opening a client takes you off the search screen. This magnifying glass in the top bar brings you back to Client Search from anywhere in the system.
So does this. The Clients icon at the top of the left rail. Either one works.
This panel is not part of Clarity. It is me. Drag it by its title bar to move it wherever suits you, or use this to pop it free of the edge. Nothing underneath it moves either way.
And this rolls it up to just the title bar. The same button brings it back, with your place kept.
Your first situation is waiting here. Read who is in front of you, then search for them the way you would on the street.

interstitial.title: From finding to verifying
interstitial.html:
That is the search half. You now have every documented way in: a name fragment, a year, four digits of an SSN, an alternate spelling, a term added to narrow, and a term swapped when nothing came back.

Finding a candidate record is not the same as finding the right one. The rest of this lesson is verifying: proving a record belongs to the person in front of you, and deciding what to do when more than one does.

sections.closing:
You searched on a name fragment, on a year, on four digits of a Social Security Number, and on a name that had been typed a different way. You narrowed a search that returned too much, and you swapped an identifier when a search returned nothing.

Finding a candidate record is not the same as finding the right one. That is what comes next.

tasks.title: The name he gave you
tasks.situation: A man at the front desk says "Everyone calls me Lefty. Lefty Torres. I stayed here last winter." You type Lefty. Nothing comes back.
tasks.instruction: Find his record and open it.
tasks.hint: The name he gave you is not the name on the record, and no alias was ever recorded for him. Drop it and search the last name on its own. Tor is enough.
tasks.feedback: An empty result is not proof that someone is new. He is filed under his legal name, Michael Torres, with no alias on the record. Ask what else a participant has been called. A middle name, a second last name, a nickname, a shortening. Confirm the spelling of each. Typing Lefty Torres fails too: every word must match, so a word that matches nothing guarantees an empty list.

tasks.title: When the last name may have changed
tasks.situation: A woman says everyone calls her Kate. She thinks her record may be under a former married name but is not sure which. She knows she was born in 1985.
tasks.hint: Start from one piece of information you trust. A year works on its own: 1985, or just 85.
tasks.feedback: She is filed as Katherine Morrison. Starting from a single reliable fact is the documented approach, and a year alone narrows three hundred records to a list you can read by eye.

tasks.title: Starting from the last four of the SSN
tasks.situation: A woman gives her name as Danielle and the last four of her Social Security Number: 7742. She is not sure how her last name was spelled when she enrolled.
tasks.hint: Search the four digits on their own. Two people share them. Use her first name to tell them apart.
tasks.feedback: Searching the last four is one of the documented starting points, and it works even when the name is unreliable. But a four-digit fragment is not unique: two people here end 7742. Narrow with it, then confirm on something else.

wrong.name: Marcus Pell
wrong.text: That is Marcus Pell. His SSN also ends 7742. A shared fragment narrows the list; it does not decide it.

tasks.title: A name you cannot spell
tasks.situation: A man gives his name as Krzysztof Wojciechowski. You try your best guess at the spelling and get nothing.
tasks.hint: You do not need the whole name. The first few letters of each is enough. The same way kat joh finds Katherine Johnson.
tasks.feedback: Short fragments beat full names because a full name has to be spelled the way somebody else typed it and a fragment does not. krz woj reaches him immediately.

tasks.title: Too many results
tasks.situation: A woman gives her last name as Garcia. You search it and get twelve records across two pages. She tells you her first name is Esperanza.
tasks.instruction: Narrow the search and open her record.
tasks.hint: Add a second term rather than starting again. Last name plus the first few letters of the first name will do it.
tasks.feedback: When a search returns more than you can read, add another term. A first name, a middle name, a second last name, an SSN fragment, a date of birth. Adding narrows; you rarely need to start over.

tasks.title: Nothing comes back
tasks.situation: A man says he is Adrian Fenwick and gives his date of birth as 04/12/1988. Searching that date returns nothing. He also remembers the last four of his SSN: 5518.
tasks.hint: When a search returns nothing, replace one piece of information with another rather than adding to it. Swap the date of birth for the SSN fragment.
tasks.feedback: His record holds 12/04/1988. The month and day are the other way round, which is how dates get mistyped everywhere. When you get nothing, swap an identifier rather than piling more on: date of birth for last four of the SSN, first name for last.

tasks.title: Spelled the way someone else heard it
tasks.situation: A woman introduces herself as Cathleen Brennan. Searching Cathleen returns nothing.
tasks.hint: A previous provider may have written it down differently. Try the other spelling of that first sound.
tasks.feedback: She is filed as Kathleen. The swaps worth trying first are the ones people make without noticing: C and K, I and Y. Catherine and Katherine, Jonson and Johnson. Try the alternate spelling before you conclude anyone is new.

tasks.title: A surname typed as one word
tasks.situation: A caseworker asks you to pull up Maria de la Cruz. You search Cruz, then Maria Cruz. Both come back empty.
tasks.hint: Her last name was typed as a single word. Search the fragment common to every spelling: dela. Or drop the last name and search her first name.
tasks.feedback: She is filed as Maria Delacruz, one word. Search matches from the start of a name, so Cruz never reaches it. Second last names and compound last names get entered differently by every agency. Search the distinctive fragment, or the first name.

sections.title: Practice: Verifying a Record
sections.closing: You told two people with the same name apart on a second identifier. You identified someone whose record held almost no identifiers, using her household. You confirmed another on where he had been staying. You chose between three records that all matched. And you found someone the identifiers could not reach at all, from a fragment, a year, and one thing he mentioned in passing.

tasks.title: Two people, one name
tasks.situation: A man says he is James Wilson. He gives his date of birth as 9/2/1968 and the last four of his SSN as 4471.
tasks.hint: Narrow it with what he told you. The fragment 4471, or the date of birth. Or read the SSN and DOB columns and compare.
tasks.feedback: These are two different people. As a rule of thumb, a record is a match when at least two of the three (name, date of birth, SSN) match the participant. A name on its own is never enough.

wrong.name: James Wilson
wrong.text: That is the other James Wilson. Born 4/17/1991, SSN ending 9038. Two records sharing a name are not automatically duplicates.

tasks.title: When the identifiers are thin
tasks.situation: A woman says her name is Yolanda Amari. She does not know her Social Security Number and is unsure of her exact date of birth. She mentions her daughter, Iris, who is with her.
tasks.instruction: Open the record that belongs to the mother.
tasks.hint: Search the last name, then open a row's chevron to see its household members. The record you want lists Iris.
tasks.feedback: When name, date of birth, and SSN cannot settle it, the record holds other things you can confirm with the participant: household members, program history, case notes, location, veteran status. Here the household is what identifies her.

wrong.name: Iris Amari
wrong.text: That is Iris, the daughter. You are looking for the record that lists Iris as a household member, not Iris's own record.

tasks.title: Where they have been staying
tasks.situation: A man gives his name as David Nguyen. Two records come back. Both David Nguyen, both born in 1982. He does not know his Social Security Number and cannot remember which agency he last worked with. He does tell you he has been staying by the wash under the 6th Street bridge, and has been for about a year.
tasks.instruction: Open the record whose location history matches where he has been staying.
tasks.hint: Name and date of birth cannot separate these two. Open each record, go to the Location tab, and compare. One of them has been contacted at the 6th Street bridge.
tasks.feedback: When name and date of birth cannot separate two records, the rest of the record can. In outreach, location is often the fastest of them: where someone has been contacted before is a fact you can both check, and it does not ask the participant to remember an agency name or a date. Confirm it with them rather than assuming. People move, and a location recorded a year ago proves less than one recorded last month. Treat it as one identifier among several, not as the answer on its own.

tasks.title: Everything at once
tasks.situation: A man introduces himself as Smoke. It is the only name anyone out here uses for him. Pressed, he gives a last name. Reyes, he thinks, though it might have been written down as Reyez or Rios. He does not know his date of birth beyond the year, 1971, and he will not give a Social Security Number. He does tell you he served. Army, a long time ago.
tasks.instruction: Find his record and open it.
tasks.hint: Nothing you have been given finds him on its own. The first three letters are the same in all three spellings. Search Rey, then use the year and the Veteran Status column to cut the list down.
tasks.feedback: This is the real thing. No date of birth, no Social Security Number, a street name that is on no record, and a last name three plausible spellings deep. What is left is a fragment, a year, and one fact he volunteered. He is filed as Elias Reyez. Veteran status is worth remembering precisely because it is the kind of thing people tell you without being asked. When the identifiers are thin, the thing they mentioned in passing is often what closes it. And notice what you did not do: you did not conclude he was new because a search came back empty. You cleared the box and typed something else, and then did it again.

tasks.title: More than one record matches
tasks.situation: You search Vega and find three records. All three are Rosalind Vega, born 4/11/1983. All three appear to be the same person.
tasks.instruction: Open the record you would work from.
tasks.hint: Choose the most complete one. Full SSN, full date of birth, full name, an alias, the fullest history. Open a row's chevron and the record page to compare.
tasks.feedback: Work from the most complete record. Full SSN, full date of birth, full name, full program history. Where that is unclear, take the one with the longest enrollment history, based on the oldest enrollment. Note the Unique Identifiers of the others as you go, so you are not starting from nothing if it comes up again.

wrong.name: Rosalind Vega
wrong.text: That record has only a partial SSN and no alias. A more complete record exists.

wrong.name: Rosalind Vega
wrong.text: That record has no SSN on file at all, and it is the newest. A more complete record exists.

phases.happens: An empty list is not proof this person has no record.
Two records. Both Dezmond, both born that year, neither with a Social Security Number on file. Nothing he has told you separates them.

phases.does: Opens each record in turn and compares the Location tab and the Point of Contact against what he has said.

feedback.title: Not this client
feedback.body: That isn't the participant described in the task. Close the profile and refine your search.

feedback.title: Wrong record
feedback.body: That record isn't part of the duplicate pair described in this task.

feedback.title: Not a duplicate
feedback.body: Flagging is for records that appear to describe the same person twice. This task asks you to find and open one specific client.

feedback.title: No results is not an answer
feedback.body: An empty list is not proof this person has no record. Before you conclude that, try a shorter fragment of the name, the surname instead of the first name, or the year of birth on its own.

panel.hover: This panel is mine, not Clarity's. Drag it by the title bar to move it anywhere. Pop out lifts it off the edge; collapse rolls it up to the title bar. Neither moves the interface, and neither loses your place.
panel.habit: An empty result is not proof that someone is new. Search the surname fragment, search the year of birth, confirm on a second identifier — and only then create a record.
